title: The Indian Labour Conference: where Government, employers and unions meet
author: Editorial Desk
summary: A tripartite forum that has shaped wage policy for decades.
body:
The **Indian Labour Conference (ILC)** is the Government's tripartite consultative body on labour. Government, employers' organisations and central trade unions sit together to discuss questions of labour policy. Its idea comes from the same principle as the International Labour Organization's tripartism, namely that those who make labour policy should hear the people it affects before they decide. It is sometimes called the "Labour Parliament of India", though it has no power to legislate. This post explains what the Conference is, which of its sessions mattered, why unions keep returning to its recommendations, and what readers should check when a headline says that the Government has "consulted" trade unions.

## What the Conference is

The ILC is the apex forum in India for dialogue between the Government, employers and workers. The Union Labour Minister chairs it, and a smaller tripartite body, the **Standing Labour Committee**, helps to prepare its agenda. Reference works record that the first Conference was held in 1942, during British rule, and that it has met 46 times as of the sessions before 2025. It is convened by the Labour Ministry from time to time and not on a fixed annual schedule, so there have been long gaps. The Ministry's own agenda notes for the 46th session show that it met in New Delhi on 20 and 21 July 2015, and the sessions listed in the sources I consulted do not go beyond that one.

The Conference is advisory. Its conclusions are recommendations to the Government, and it is then for the Government to act. That is why unions measure its worth not only by what it says but by what the Government does with it.

## The 15th session (1957): the need-based minimum wage

The 15th session was held in New Delhi in July 1957, and its norms are still quoted by unions. It laid down guidelines for fixing a **need-based minimum wage**. A standard working-class family was taken as three consumption units for one earner. The food requirement was set at 2,700 calories per adult, clothing at 18 yards per person per year (72 yards for a family of four), and housing at the rent for the minimum area under the Government's industrial housing scheme. Fuel, lighting and other items were to be 20 per cent of the minimum wage. Where a minimum was set below these norms, the authorities were expected to justify why.

The same session recommended tripartite wage boards, adopted a model agreement on rationalisation that sought to protect workers from retrenchment and loss of earnings, started a sub-committee that drafted the **Code of Discipline**, and launched an experiment in workers' participation in management in 50 voluntary units. The Code of Discipline was adopted at the 16th session at Nainital in 1958 and was treated as in force from 1 June 1958. It committed the parties to settle disputes through negotiation and conciliation and set out criteria for the recognition of unions, including a 15 per cent membership threshold.

## The 45th session (2013): scheme workers

The 45th session was held on 17 and 18 May 2013. Its committees discussed employment and employability, the service conditions and social security of scheme workers, social security with assured pension for all workers, and labour law for micro and small enterprises. Among its recommendations was that scheme workers, such as anganwadi workers, ASHAs and mid-day meal cook-cum-helpers, should be recognised as workers and paid minimum wages. An action-taken report prepared for the 46th session records that the ministries concerned said anganwadi workers and mid-day meal cook-cum-helpers could not be treated as workers, and described ASHAs as honorary workers who receive performance-based incentives. The same report records that a monthly minimum pension of Rs 1,000 under the Employees' Pension Scheme 1995 was notified with effect from 1 September 2014.

This is a useful example of why trade unions keep returning to the recommendation. A tripartite consensus was recorded, yet its central point on scheme workers was not implemented, and unions still cite it.

## The 46th session (2015)

The 46th session, held on 20 and 21 July 2015, had five agenda items: the implementation of the conclusions of the 43rd, 44th and 45th sessions, particularly on contract labour, minimum wages, scheme workers and the tripartite mechanism; social security for workers in the organised and unorganised sectors and for international migrant workers; amendment of the Bonus Act; labour law amendments proposed or made by the Central or State Governments; and employment and employment generation. The agenda shows the Conference at its purpose: reviewing whether earlier agreements had been carried out.

## Other forums where unions are consulted

The Conference is not the only place where the Government meets unions. The Standing Labour Committee, tripartite meetings on specific subjects, pre-legislative consultations on draft laws and wage boards all provide occasions. These forums differ in size, in formal weight and in who is invited, which is why the form of consultation matters.

## BMS and tripartism

BMS has regularly argued that labour laws should be made after genuine tripartite consultation, that the consensus reached in the Conference should be respected, and that the Conference should meet regularly and not at long intervals. Its concern is practical. When a law affecting millions of workers is prepared, the workers' side wants to examine the text, to propose changes, and to see that an agreement reached at one table is not undone elsewhere.

## What readers should check

If a headline says "Government consults unions", ask four questions:

- **Which forum is it?** The Indian Labour Conference, the Standing Labour Committee, a ministerial meeting with a few unions and an online comments window are very different things.
- **Who attended?** A meeting with a few unions is different from a full tripartite session with all the central trade unions and employers' organisations.
- **Was there a draft to discuss?** Consultation on a finished text is not the same as consultation on a proposal.
- **What was recorded?** Whether minutes, conclusions and dissent are published tells you how seriously the process is taken.

## What remains

The 1957 norms are still quoted because they gave a reasoned method for deciding what a wage should cover. The 2013 recommendation on scheme workers is still quoted because it was not implemented. A Conference that meets rarely cannot do either job, so the demand for regular sessions with published conclusions is a modest and a sensible one. Regular tripartite dialogue is not a favour to unions. It is how a law that affects workers can be tested before it takes effect.
